title: Lights and fans in a home
short: Every room needs enough light and enough air movement. Light is counted in lumens and fans by blade size (sweep). A normal Indian home needs a few LED bulbs or tubes and one ceiling fan per room, with the size depending on the room.
points: Lights: add up the brightness the room needs (lux) times its floor area, then divide by what one lamp gives (lumens).
Fans: pick the sweep by room size. About 900 mm for a small room up to 100 sq ft, 1200 mm for a medium room, 1400 mm for a hall.
Power: an LED bulb uses about 9 W, an LED tube about 20 W, a regular ceiling fan about 75 W and a BLDC fan about 28 W.
Cost: the fan usually costs more to run than the lights, because it runs many hours a day.

title: How much light a room needs
short: Brightness is measured in lumens (how much light a lamp gives) and lux (how much of it lands on each square metre of floor). A room needs a target lux, and the number of lamps follows from the room size.
points: Lumens needed = target lux × floor area in m² ÷ (0.5 × 0.8). The 0.5 and 0.8 allow for light lost on walls and for dust and ageing.
Typical targets (lower end of the building-code range): living room 100 lux, bedroom 75, bathroom 150, kitchen 300.
Then lamps = lumens needed ÷ lumens per lamp, rounded up.
Do not compare lamps by watts. Compare by lumens, because an LED gives much more light per watt than an old bulb.

title: LED, CFL and old bulbs
short: An LED gives the same light for about one-sixth to one-tenth of the power of an old filament bulb, and it lasts much longer. That is why a 9 W LED replaces a 60 W bulb.
points: Old filament bulb: roughly 12 to 15 lumens per watt, most of the power becomes heat.
CFL and fluorescent tubes: roughly 50 to 70 lumens per watt (an old tube also needs a choke that uses a little power).
LED: roughly 80 to 120 lumens per watt in good products.
Cheap LEDs can be worse than the label says, so look for a known brand and check the lumens, not only the watts.

title: Ceiling fans: size, speed and power
short: A ceiling fan is chosen by sweep, the width of the circle its blades make. A bigger room needs a bigger sweep or two fans. A regular fan uses about 75 W, and a BLDC (inverter) fan uses about 28 W for similar air.
points: Rule of thumb for sweep: up to 100 sq ft about 900 mm, 100 to 150 sq ft about 1050 mm, 150 to 225 sq ft about 1200 mm, 225 to 300 sq ft about 1400 mm, bigger rooms use two fans.
Hang the fan at least 2.4 m (8 ft) above the floor and 0.3 m or more below the ceiling.
More blades or a bigger sweep does not always mean more air. Check the air delivery (CMM) on the box.
A 5-star rated non-BLDC fan uses about 40 to 50 W.

title: BLDC (inverter) fans and why they save power
short: A BLDC fan has an electronic motor that wastes much less power than the old coil motor. It does the same job at roughly 28 W instead of 75 W, so it pays back its higher price in a few years if it runs many hours.
points: Saving per fan per month = (75 W − 28 W) × hours a day × 30 ÷ 1000 units. At 10 hours a day that is about 14 units.
With several fans running through summer, the saving is noticeable on the bill.
Most come with a remote and a speed control.
numbers: about 14 per month at 10 h a day

title: Units, kWh and how your electricity bill is made
short: The meter counts units. One unit is one kilowatt-hour: a 1,000 W load running for one hour. Your bill is the units used times the tariff for that unit, plus fixed charges and taxes that your state adds.
points: Units per month = watts × hours a day × 30 ÷ 1000, added up for every appliance.
Tariffs are usually in slabs: the first units cost less and later units cost more, and they differ by state. Use the rate on your own bill.
A bill also has a fixed or demand charge and duties, so the cost per unit on the bill is higher than the slab rate.
To check an estimate, compare it with the units on your real bill. This is what the compare option does.

title: Watts, amps and volts
short: Power in watts equals voltage times current: P = V × I. A home runs at 230 V, so a 2,000 W geyser draws about 8.7 A. The amps decide the wire and breaker size.
points: Amps = watts ÷ 230 for a home appliance.
Ohm’s law links them: voltage = current × resistance.
Add up the amps of what runs together to see if a circuit is overloaded.
A breaker rated 6 A is for lights and fans, 16 A for sockets, 20 to 25 A for AC or geyser.
tryit: MCB and wire size for a 2000 W geyser

title: MCB: the switch that protects your wiring
short: An MCB (miniature circuit breaker) switches off a circuit when too much current flows, so the wire does not overheat. Its rating must be lower than what the wire can carry and higher than what the load normally draws.
points: Common sizes: 6, 10, 16, 20, 25, 32, 40, 63 A. Pick the next size above 1.25 × the load current.
Lights and fans: 6 A. Sockets: 16 A. AC or geyser: 20 to 25 A on their own circuit.
Curves: B trips early (good for lights and heaters), C is the common choice for homes and small motors, D is for big inrush loads.
An MCB protects the wire from overload. It does not protect a person from shock. For that you need an RCCB or ELCB.

title: Wire size: why thicker wire for bigger loads
short: A wire heats up as current flows through it. A thicker wire has less resistance, so it stays cool and carries more current. Choosing the wire size by load keeps it safe and avoids voltage drop on long runs.
points: Common house sizes: 1.5 mm² for lights and fans, 2.5 mm² for sockets, 4 mm² for AC, 6 mm² for heavy geysers or a main feed.
Use copper wire from a known maker and keep the colour code (red/yellow/blue for phases, black for neutral, green for earth).
Long runs need a thicker wire to avoid voltage drop.
The breaker must always be smaller than what the wire can carry.

title: Earthing, RCCB and shock protection
short: Earthing gives leaked current a safe path to the ground so it does not go through you. An RCCB (or ELCB) cuts the power in a fraction of a second when it senses a leak, usually at 30 milliamps, which protects people.
points: Every metal-body appliance (fridge, washing machine, geyser, AC) needs a working earth wire.
The RCCB goes at the incoming side of the board. Test it with its test button every month.
If you feel a tingle when you touch an appliance, switch it off and call an electrician. Do not ignore it.
An MCB and an RCCB do different jobs. You want both.

title: Air conditioners at home: tonnage, stars and units
short: AC size is quoted in tons. One ton of cooling is about 3.5 kW of heat removed, but the AC itself uses much less electricity, roughly 1 to 1.5 kW for a 1.5 ton unit. A higher star rating means less electricity for the same cooling.
points: A rough rule is about one ton for 100 to 150 sq ft of room, more if the room gets strong sun or many people.
Set the thermostat to 24 to 26 °C. Each degree higher saves roughly 3 to 6% of the AC’s power.
Inverter ACs slow down instead of switching off, which saves power at part load.
Clean the filter every few weeks in summer. A dirty filter wastes electricity.
numbers: about 12,000 BTU/h or 3.5 kW of cooling

title: Geysers and water heaters
short: A geyser turns electricity straight into heat, so it is one of the biggest loads in a home. A typical one is 2,000 W and should have its own 16 A circuit with 2.5 to 4 mm² wire.
points: Instant geysers (3 kW) heat quickly but draw more current. Storage geysers (1.5 to 2 kW) heat slowly and keep the water hot.
Use a timer or switch it on 15 to 20 minutes before you need hot water, and switch it off after.
It needs an earth wire and an RCCB on the circuit.
Energy: 2,000 W for 30 minutes is 1 unit.

title: Refrigerators and their electricity use
short: A fridge runs all day but its compressor works only part of the time. The BEE label gives its yearly energy use. A direct-cool 220 L fridge is about 107 kWh a year and a frost-free 300 L about 160 kWh, according to a buying guide.
points: That is only about 9 to 13 units a month, so a fridge is a small part of the bill.
Keep it away from the wall and heat, do not put hot food in, and clean the back coils.
More stars means less power for the same size.

title: Inverters, batteries and backup time
short: Backup hours depend on the battery energy and your load. Battery energy is volts times amp-hours, but you can use only about half of it and the inverter loses some. Then divide by the watts you run.
points: Backup time = battery volts × Ah × usable share (about 0.5) × inverter efficiency (about 0.85) ÷ load in watts.
A 12 V 150 Ah battery with a 300 W load gives about 2.5 hours by this method.
Run only fans and lights on inverter. ACs and geysers drain it very fast.
tryit: battery backup 12 V 150 Ah 300 W

title: Single phase and three phase supply
short: Most flats and small houses have a single-phase supply at 230 V. Larger homes, shops and motors use three phases at 415 V between lines, which spreads big loads more evenly.
points: Single phase suits loads up to about 5 to 7 kW.
Three phase suits large ACs, pumps and workshops, and gives a steadier supply.
The number of kW you can run is limited by your sanctioned load, which is on your connection.

source.title: Three-phase electric power · Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Simple ways to lower the bill
short: The biggest savings usually come from the AC, the geyser and the fans, because they use the most units. Changing habits and a few appliances beats chasing small loads.
points: AC: set 24 to 26 °C, clean filters, close doors, switch off when away. Each degree higher saves roughly 3 to 6%.
Fans: a BLDC fan saves about 14 units a month if it runs 10 hours a day.
Lights: replace old bulbs and tubes with LEDs.
Geyser: use a timer and keep it off when not needed.
Check the stars on a new appliance. More stars means fewer units.

title: What HVAC means
short: HVAC stands for heating, ventilation and air conditioning. It is the system that keeps a building at a comfortable temperature, humidity and air quality, using ducts, pipes, fans, pumps and cooling machines.
points: Cooling comes from an air conditioner or a chiller that removes heat from the air or from water.
Ventilation brings in fresh air and takes out stale air.
Ducts carry air, pipes carry chilled water, and fans and pumps move them.
Sizing each part correctly is the main job: too small cannot cool, too big wastes money and controls humidity badly.
tryit: How many tons of AC do I need for a 20 by 15 m office with 80 people?

title: Ton of refrigeration (TR)
short: A ton of refrigeration is a unit of cooling power. One ton removes 12,000 BTU of heat per hour, which is about 3.517 kW. It comes from the old days when cooling was compared with melting a ton of ice in a day.
points: kW of cooling ÷ 3.517 = tons. Tons × 3.517 = kW of cooling.
This is the heat removed, not the electricity used. A good machine uses much less electricity than the cooling it gives (that ratio is the COP).
Small ACs are quoted in tons, big chillers in TR or kW.

title: CFM and how much air a system moves
short: CFM is cubic feet per minute, the volume of air moved each minute. Metric systems use m³/h or litres per second. A common rule of thumb is about 400 cfm of supply air for each ton of cooling.
points: 1 cfm is about 1.7 m³/h or 0.47 L/s.
Flow = air speed × duct area. That is how duct sizes are found.
Too little air gives warm rooms and icing coils, too much gives noise and drafts.

title: How ducts are sized
short: A duct is sized from the airflow and the speed you want the air to move. Area equals flow divided by speed, and the round diameter follows from the area. Higher speed gives a smaller duct but more noise and fan power.
points: Diameter = √(4 × flow ÷ (π × velocity)).
Common design speeds in office branch ducts are about 4 to 6 m/s, and main ducts can be faster. Quiet spaces need lower speeds.
Then the next standard size is chosen, and the real speed is rechecked.
Long runs, bends and dampers add pressure loss, which the fan must overcome.

title: What cooling load is and how it is estimated
short: Cooling load is how much heat must be removed to keep a space at the right temperature. It comes from people, lights, equipment, sunshine through glass and heat through walls and the roof, plus fresh air.
points: A quick estimate multiplies floor area by a watts-per-m² figure for the type of space, and adds for people.
A full design calculation (ASHRAE or Manual J style) is needed before ordering big equipment.
Sensible load changes the temperature, latent load is moisture (see sensible and latent heat).

title: COP, EER and efficiency of cooling machines
short: COP (coefficient of performance) is cooling delivered divided by electricity used. A COP of 3.5 means 3.5 kW of cooling for each 1 kW of electricity. EER is the same ratio in BTU per hour per watt, so EER = COP × 3.412.
points: A higher COP means a cheaper machine to run.
kW per ton = 3.517 ÷ COP. A COP of 3.5 is about 1 kW per ton.
Seasonal ratings (SEER, ISEER) average the efficiency over a typical year, including part load.
numbers: EER about 12 and 1.0 kW per ton

title: Dew point, humidity and condensation
short: Dew point is the temperature at which the moisture in the air starts to turn into water. If a duct, pipe or window is colder than the dew point of the air touching it, water forms on it. Relative humidity says how close the air is to that limit.
points: Comfort is usually best between 40 and 60% relative humidity.
Chilled-water pipes and cold ducts need insulation so they stay above the dew point and do not drip.
Cooling coils work below the dew point on purpose, which is how air conditioners dry the air.

title: Psychrometrics and the psychrometric chart
short: Psychrometrics is the study of moist air. A psychrometric chart shows dry-bulb temperature, humidity, dew point and enthalpy (heat content) together, so you can follow what happens as air is cooled, heated or dried.
points: Give it any two properties, such as temperature and relative humidity, and the others follow.
Enthalpy tells how much heat the air carries, which sizes the cooling coil.
The calculator here gives dew point, humidity ratio, enthalpy and vapour pressure.

title: Sensible and latent heat
short: Sensible heat changes the temperature of the air. Latent heat is the energy in water vapour, which changes the humidity without changing the temperature. An air conditioner has to remove both.
points: Sensible heat comes from people, lights, equipment and the sun.
Latent heat comes from people breathing, cooking and fresh air in a humid climate.
Sensible heat ratio (SHR) is the share that is sensible. Humid places need machines that remove more moisture.

title: Chilled water, delta T and pipe size
short: In bigger buildings a chiller cools water, and pipes carry it to coils in air handlers. The cooling it can deliver depends on the water flow and how much it warms up (delta T). Flow = cooling kW ÷ (4.186 × delta T).
points: Typical delta T is about 5 to 6 K, for example water leaving at 7 °C and returning at 12 °C.
A bigger delta T needs less water and smaller pipes, but the coils must be designed for it.
Pipes are sized so the water speed is moderate, usually around 1 to 3 m/s, to limit noise and friction.
tryit: Chilled water pipe size for 300 kW at 5 degree delta T

title: Motor current and breaker size
short: A motor draws a full-load current set by its power, voltage and efficiency. The breaker must be larger than that so it does not trip when running, but small enough to protect the cable. A common start is 125% of the full-load current, then the next standard size.
points: Three-phase current ≈ kW × 1000 ÷ (√3 × voltage × power factor × efficiency).
A motor draws several times its running current for a moment when it starts, which a starter or VFD can reduce.
Always check the motor nameplate and the local code for the final choice.
tryit: Breaker for a 15 kW motor, 415 V, 3 phase

title: Power factor
short: Power factor tells how much of the current does useful work. It is kW divided by kVA. Motors and transformers push it below 1, which makes cables and supply equipment carry more current than the useful power needs.
points: Motors are often about 0.8 to 0.9 at full load.
A capacitor bank can raise it, and many utilities charge extra for low power factor in industry.
Real power (kW) = voltage × current × power factor for single phase.

title: Fan and pump laws, and why VFDs save energy
short: For fans and pumps, flow changes in proportion to speed, pressure with the square of speed, and power with the cube of speed. So running at 80% speed uses only about half the power, which is why a variable frequency drive (VFD) saves so much.
points: At 80% speed: flow 80%, pressure 64%, power about 51%.
This only holds when the system resistance does not change, which is true for most duct and pipe systems.
Slowing a fan with a damper wastes power, a VFD does not.

title: Basic HVAC care: filters, coils and drains
short: Most AC problems come from dirt and neglect. Dirty filters cut airflow, dirty coils cut cooling and raise the power bill, and a blocked drain leaks water.
points: Clean or change filters every month or two in heavy use.
Clean condenser and evaporator coils at least once or twice a year.
Check the drain pipe, refrigerant pressures and electrical connections during a service.
You can ask for a reminder, for example: remind me to clean the condenser at site B every 3 months.
